record.provider: IPFS Foundation public gateways (ipfs.io / dweb.link / trustless-gateway.link)

free_tier.stated: No storage at all. Gateway only. And the gateway itself is being retired: ipfs.io/dweb.link return HTTP 429 with 'Retry-After: 900' and 'Sunset: Mon, 21 Sep 2026', and redirect browsers to inbrowser.link.

egress.terms: Rate-limited to the point of unusability from a datacenter IP: 10/10 requests returned 429 on a cold burst, and a single request after a 5 s pause also returned 429. Published posture: 'Rate limiting has begun on ipfs.io and dweb.link for hotlinked and backend traffic, and will be increasing.' Docs: 'no SLA, no support, and shared rate limits that can throttle or block your traffic at any time, without notice.'

record.tooling: curl/any HTTP client; path gateway at ipfs.io, subdomain at dweb.link; trustless subset at trustless-gateway.link.
record.chaining: none. The three hostnames are one backend: 'They are not three separate services... sharing the same cache, the same connections to the IPFS network, and the same rate limits.' Rotating hostnames burns the same budget.
record.limits_note: 429 + Retry-After 900 observed on the first request; Range requests capped at 5 GiB (Cloudflare CDN limit); Sunset header 2026-09-21.
record.reliability_note: This is the single most important measurement in the slot: the 'free IPFS CDN' that every tutorial assumes is (a) gone as of 2026-09-21 and (b) already 429-ing datacenter IPs before that date. Any architecture that depends on ipfs.io/dweb.link for serving is dead on arrival.

evidence.proved: probe: GET -> HTTP/1.1 429, Retry-After: 900, Link: rel="sunset", Sunset: Mon, 21 Sep 2026; 10/10 subsequent requests 429
(2026-08-25) — 'Rate limiting has begun on ipfs.io and dweb.link for hotlinked and backend traffic, and will be increasing.'
'these pauses keep growing until it retires for good on September 21 (UTC)'

card.summary: Storage and egress are whatever your VPS/host allows. No provider quota exists. The cost moves to the host's bandwidth allowance.

free_tier.stated: Storage and egress are whatever your VPS/host allows. No provider quota exists. The cost moves to the host's bandwidth allowance.

egress.terms: Host bandwidth is paid directly to the server provider. IPFS documentation recommends fronting gateways with caching CDNs using standard Cache-Control, ETag, and X-Ipfs-Roots headers to minimize origin bandwidth consumption.

record.tooling: Kubo (go-ipfs), Rainbow (github.com/ipfs/rainbow), Someguy for delegated routing, Helia in-browser; rclone can talk to the Kubo RPC API via a webdav/MFS shim but there is no first-class rclone backend.
record.chaining: Does not multiply free storage. It only re-serves content you already paid to pin. Combined with a free pinning service it can turn 5 GB of free pinning into unmetered-looking reads, but only for 5 GB of content.
record.limits_note: Bandwidth of the VPS; DHT lookup latency on cold CIDs; no excess-use protection by default ('Unlike ipfs.io, a self-hosted gateway has no abuse protection by default').
record.reliability_note: This is the honest answer to 'does self-hosting change the economics?': it changes who meters you, not whether you are metered. It just moves the bill to the VPS or CDN.

evidence.proved: 'Put a CDN like Cloudflare in front of the IPFS gateway'; 'a self-hosted gateway has no abuse protection by default' (the vendor means it applies no excess-use protection)
'Ensure that you are correctly returning HTTP cache headers... Consider leveraging the list of CIDs in X-Ipfs-Roots'
